So absent any specific agreement between the parties (or other special circumstances) the “without prejudice” privilege is presumed to expire once the merits of the dispute have been decided. [Emphasis added]. 24 I do not read Mahe as creating a general rule for litigation privilege. First, the Court refers to both litigation privilege and “without prejudice” privilege, instead of lumping both together. Second, by discussing “without prejudice” privilege by citing the rule in Blank v. Canada (Minister of Justice), 2006 SCC 39, [2006] 2 S.C.R. 319 the Court was specifically explaining that the privilege attached to settlement offers is an aspect of litigation privilege governed by unique policy considerations created by the double costs rules: see Rule 4.29 of Alberta Rules Of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010. For Rule 4.29 to operate the Court must be informed as to what the offer actually was. Mahe speaks to the privilege concerning “without prejudice” settlement discussions. (xii) Litigation privilege does not apply to sworn statements Among the large number of interviews made, five alone resulted in a sworn statement by the witness. Presumably that means an affidavit. An affidavit not intended to be used in judicial proceedings has somewhat shaky legality. Tying down someone who may later testify in court by having him privately swear to certain facts is an undesirable practice which needs no encouragement by the courts. In our view, a sworn witness statement is not something to which litigation privilege (sometimes called solicitor's brief privilege) should extend. Those five sworn statements are producible …Esso Resources Canada Ltd. v. Stearns Catalytic Ltd. (1991), 80 Alta. L.R. (2d) 264 at 265 (C.A.). (xiii) Notes made at request of lawyer In Kendall Estate (Re), 2024 ABKB 729, Justice Marion discussed when notes made at the request of a lawyer would attract privilege. He said: [54] This claim raises the issue of whether and when a lawyer's client can claim solicitor-client privilege over their personal notes. David's position appears to be that it is enough to show that notes were created at the request of and/or following the advice of counsel. In my view, it is not that simple. [55] Solicitor-client privilege exists where: (i) communications between solicitor and client; (ii) entail the seeking or giving of legal advice; and (iii) are intended to be confidential by the parties: Hirch v Lethbridge, 2024 ABCA 170 at para 26 [Hirch] citing Solosky v The Queen, 1979 CanLII 9 (SCC), [1980] 1 SCR 821 at 837 and Pritchard v Ontario (Human Rights Commission), 2004 SCC 31 at para 15 [Pritchard]. Solicitor-client privilege is permanent: Blank at 37; Lizotte v Aviva Insurance Company of Canada, 2016 SCC 52 at para 22. [56] Solicitor-client privilege is broadly interpreted and is not easily set aside: Blank at para 50; CNOOC Petroleum North America ULC v 801 Seventh Inc, 2021 ABQB 861 at paras 30 - 39 (CNOOC v 801). This is to support the privilege's fundamental purposes to allow for and to protect free and frank communications between client and lawyer, facilitating access to justice, recognizing the inherent value of personal autonomy, and affirming the efficacy of the adversarial process: Blank at para 26; R v McClure, 2001 SCC 14 at para 2; CNOOC v 801 at para 25; General Accident Assurance Company v Chrusz, 1999 CanLII 7320 (ON CA), 1999 CarswellOnt 2898 (ONCA) at para 94; Alberta (Municipal Affairs) v Alberta (Information and Privacy Commissioner), 2019 ABQB 274 at para 7; Prosser v Industrial Alliance Insurance, 2024 ABKB 87 at paras 49-50 [Prosser]. [57] Solicitor-client privilege applies to all interactions between a client and his or her lawyer when the lawyer is engaged in providing legal advice: Canada (Privacy Commissioner) v Blood Tribe Department of Health, 2008 SCC 44 at para 10. It can arise as soon as the potential client takes the first steps, even before a retainer is formalized: Pritchard at para 16, citing Descôteaux v Mierzwinski, 1982 CanLII 22 (SCC), [1982] 1 SCR 860 at p 893. [58] Solicitor-client privilege encompasses not just the request for advice and the advice itself, but a “continuum” encompassing all communications “directly related to the seeking, formulating or giving of legal advice”: Hirch at para 30; TransAlta Corporation v Alberta (Environment and Parks), 2024 ABCA 127 at para 28 [TransAlta]; Blood Tribe v Canada (Attorney General), 2010 ABCA 112 at para 26. This “continuum” aspect of solicitor-client privilege has been described as “evolving law”: CNOOC Petroleum North America ULC v 801 Seventh Inc, 2022 ABCA 293 at para 4. [59] Solicitor-client privilege can apply even if the communication is a communication of “facts”: Hirch at para 37; Canada (Attorney General) v Chambre des notaires du Québec, 2016 SCC 20 at para 40; Gault Estate v Gault Estate, 2016 ABCA 208 at para 12 [Gault Estate]. Attempting distinctions between “fact” and “communication” runs the risk of emasculating the privilege: Gault Estate at para 12, citing Maranda v Richer, 2003 SCC 67 at para 31. For example, even if someone's state of mind “could be described as a “fact”, solicitor-client privilege must extend to [the client's] discussions with [their] solicitor about that state of mind”: Gault Estate at para 13. [60] The broad interpretation of solicitor-client privilege does not mean the privilege can be made through bare or broad assertions. As noted above, the onus is on the party claiming privilege and the claim must be supported by evidence. Further, blanket claims of privilege have been rejected. ShawCor is instructive in this regard. At para 80 of ShawCor, the Court of Appeal stated: “the mere fact that a lawyer directs that all records obtained or created after a certain date must first come to him or her is not sufficient to automatically place all such records within the category of solicitor-client privilege”. One must always look at the record at issue at the time it was created, examined in the context of all the facts, the nature of the record and the real reason it was created: ShawCor at para 87. [61] Similarly, in my view, a counsel's general recommendation, direction, or instruction to a client to take notes so the lawyer can provide advice does not mean all subsequent notes taken by the client are protected by solicitor-client privilege. The party asserting privilege must establish that the elements of the privilege are met. Where there is no evidence that the notes were provided to counsel, the party must establish that they were directly related to the seeking, formulating or giving of legal advice. [62] Academic commentary and cases addressing claims of solicitor-client privilege over client notes bears out that each case relating to client notes must be considered on its own facts… …. [63] These cases reflect that if a client prepares notes at the request of counsel and provides them to counsel (or uses them to communicate with counsel), or writes notes of matters to discuss with counsel, they will likely be subject to solicitor-client privilege. However, if the notes are prepared for the client's personal use or reference, would have been made by the client anyway as part of their usual personal practice, or are never actually provided to counsel or used to assist them in communicating with counsel, they may not be privileged. Each case must be decided on its own facts. In Gilchrist v. Oatway, (1994), 22 Alta. L.R. (3d) 445 (Q.B.), a legal secretary had advised the plaintiff to keep a diary “in case the accident went further”. At p. 447, Justice Veit discussed when the resultant diary entries could be covered by privilege: The applicant states that a solicitor's brief privilege arises only when a lawyer asks a client to prepare material. Here, the diary was started at the suggestion of a friend, not the plaintiff's lawyer. Although it is usual that documents created for litigation are created at the request of a lawyer, a request by a lawyer is not a necessary prerequisite to a finding that a document was prepared for purposes of litigation. Here, the evidence of the plaintiff has been consistent: she started the diary at the suggestion of a legal secretary “in case the accident went further”. The only reasonable interpretation of the phrase, “went further” in this context is “went to litigation”. When the issue did, in fact, go further, the plaintiff's lawyer suggested that she maintain the diary. I am satisfied from the evidence that the dominant purpose of the diary was for litigation: to instruct the plaintiff's lawyer about the nature and extent of the injuries suffered. On the evidence to date, the diary was not created for the dominant purpose of being able to refresh the plaintiff's memory on discovery. (xiv) One cannot use discovery process to thwart privilege This application raises the question of what privilege attaches to the surveillance a defendant has caused to be made of a plaintiff who has sued for personal injuries sustained in a motor vehicle accident… In the present case it is clear the dominant purpose of the surveillance was for the purpose of litigation and in my opinion the documents (including the video tape) are privileged and the defendant does not have to produce them… As an alternative to production of the documents and the video, counsel for the plaintiff seeks an order compelling the defendant to answer all questions posed at an examination for discovery concerning the factual content of the document and video. The type of questions contemplated by the plaintiff's counsel include: (a) The fact that the plaintiff has been the subject matter of a surveillance. (b) The dates upon which the surveillance happened. (c) Where the surveillance took place. (d) The name of the investigator. (e) The details of what was observed. Where a document is privileged, can any question be asked about it on examination for discovery? In some jurisdictions it appears no questions may be asked. In some jurisdictions it appears a few questions can be asked. In some jurisdictions it appears that nearly any question can be asked as long as the question only seeks information about a fact and not about the evidence by which a fact is to be proved… There is not much Alberta case law dealing with this matter, but what there is supports the position that where a document is privileged the privilege should not be whittled away by compelling questions about it on an examination for discovery to be answered. McDonnell v. Lopuch (1993), 7 Alta. L.R. (3d) 407 (Master), at 408-10, per Master Quinn. Consider also the comments of the Court of Appeal in Specialty Steels v. Suncor Inc. (1997), 54 Alta. L.R. (3d) 246. They do not appear to be in conflict. Master Quinn was speaking of information which only came into existence because of the directions leading to the privileged report. In Specialty Steels v. Suncor Inc. (1997), 54 Alta. L.R. (3d) 246, the Court of Appeal was speaking of information, not otherwise privileged, which happens to be found in the report. At p. 250, the Court of Appeal said: Facts stated in the report and other documents referred to in it may or may not be privileged. Unless such facts and documents are otherwise privileged, referring to them in the report does not protect them from disclosure and they may be obtained by other means of discovery. The distinction between a document and its contents was emphasized by Jackett P. in Susan Hosiery Ltd. v. Minister of National Revenue (1969), 69 D.T.C. 5278 (Can. Ex. Ct.). He referred to the two aspects of solicitor-client privilege, namely the privilege for communications between solicitor and client and the privilege attaching to materials and documents prepared or obtained for use in existing or contemplated litigation. Citing Lord Blackburn in Kennedy v. Lyell (No. 2) (1883), 9 App. Cas. 81 (Eng. H.L.) at 86/87, Jackett P. concluded at p. 5281: What is important to note about both of these rules is that they do not afford a privilege against the discovery of facts that are or may be relevant to the determination of the facts in issue. What is privileged is the communications or working papers that came into existence by reason of the desire to obtain a legal opinion or legal assistance in the one case and the materials created for the lawyer's brief in the other case. The facts or documents that happen to be reflected in such communications or materials are not privileged from discovery if, otherwise, the party would be bound to give discovery of them. The same distinction is made in [Choate], Discovery in Canada (1st ed., Carswell, 1977) at Para. B473: Facts in the case that ought to be known by the principals, no matter how obtained, are not privileged, but documents which come into existence for the purpose of being communicated to a solicitor with the object of obtaining his advice or enabling him either to prosecute or defend an action, are privileged. (xv) Records marked “Without Prejudice”; Records marked “With Prejudice” I … would prefer to decide the matter on the basis of general principles laid down by the various authorities on the matter of without prejudice correspondence. The cases referred to in the briefs and during argument appear to be unanimous in their adoption of the conditions that must be present for privilege to attach to this type of document: (a) there must be some dispute or negotiation in existence or within contemplation; (b) the communication must be made with the express or implied intention that it would not be disclosed to the court in the event that negotiations failed; (c) the purpose of the communication must be to attempt to effect a compromise or settlement. I suppose it could be added, almost parenthetically, that the “without prejudice” endorsement on the communication is not determinative of the issue. Sopinka and Lederman, The Law of Evidence in Civil Cases, at p. 198. I think it is common ground that if a communication is marked “without prejudice” there is a prima facie presumption that it will be excluded. It is a question of whether the party wanting its inclusion can overcome the presumption. College of Physicians & Surgeons (Alberta) v. Cooper (1994), 18 Alta. L.R. (3d) 188 (Master), at 191, per Master Breitkreuz. On appeal [(1994) 38 Alta. L.R. (3d) 71 (Q.B.)], Roslak J. reached a different conclusion concerning the records being considered, but he did agree with the learned Master's explanation of the law (see pp. 74-75). In Chevron Canada Resources v. Canada (Executive Director of Indian Oil & Gas Canada) (1997), 210 A.R. 64 (Q.B.), Chief Justice Moore commented on the inablility of a party to unilaterally waive the privilege of a “without prejudice” communication. His Lordship said at p. 71: Many of the rest of the documents appended to Mr. Reader's affidavit are labelled “without prejudice”. Chevron states that it is waiving privilege for the purposes of this application. Ermineskin reminds the court that Chevron cannot unilaterally waive privilege. In Phillips v. Rodgers (1988), 62 Alta. L.R. (2d) 140 (Q.B.), Roslak, J., refused to allow one party to waive unilaterally the privilege of three “without prejudice” letters. He cited Pirie v. Wyld (1886), 11 O.R. 422 (C.A.) at 427 for the general principle that: … letters written or communications made without prejudice, or offers made for the sake of buying peace, or to effect a compromise, are inadmissible in evidence. It seemingly being considered against public policy as having a tendency to promote litigation, and to prevent amicable settlements. He cited Dunlap v. Dunlap (1985), 47 R.F.L. (2d) 247 (Man. Q.B.) at 248-249 for the principle that both parties must consent to a waiver of privilege, except in certain circumstances, such as threats or illegality. Such circumstances do not appear to be present here. In Phillips (at p. 144), Roslak, J., extended the principles to documents which, although not marked “without prejudice”, are “made as part of a process of negotiation or settlement”. However, he also stated that documents marked “without prejudice” are not always privileged. They must be part of the negotiation process to be privileged. In Newland Contracting (North) Ltd. (Receiver of) v. Rendek Developments Ltd. (2001), 93 Alta. L.R. (3d) 161 (Master), Master Quinn considered the admissibility of privileged material when the issue in dispute is the existence of an alleged settlement agreement. At pp. 164-165, the learned Master said: In McLeod v. Pearson, [1931] 3 W.W.R. 4 (Alta. T.D.) Ford, J. summarized the law concerning admissibility of letters written “without prejudice” by quoting with approval the following excerpt from 13 Halsbury's Laws of England: “634. … Moreover, the law has always been peculiarly tender in its treatment of efforts made by the parties to compromise their disputes, and accordingly it will altogether exclude proof of negotiations entered into for that purpose either expressly or impliedly ‘without prejudice’. In order, however, to entitle communications to protection on this ground, it must appear that there was a dispute or negotiation impending between them, and that the letters were written, or interviews held, bona fide with a view to its settlement. 761. Letters written during a dispute or negotiation between the parties, and expressed or otherwise proved to have been written ‘without prejudice’, cannot in general be admitted in evidence without the consent of both parties. … Where the privilege exists, it covers not only the particular letter itself, but also all subsequent parts of the same correspondence on both sides, notwithstanding that they are not expressed to be ‘without prejudice’. … The court may look at a document written ‘without prejudice’ for the purposes of deciding the question of admissibility.” This case shows the importance attached by Alberta Courts to negotiations concerning settlements which are made without prejudice. It does not however answer the particular question of whether privileged material may be admitted in evidence where the very question in dispute is the existence of a settlement agreement and there is no consent of both parties for the privileged material to be admitted in evidence. I am unaware of any Alberta case dealing with the particular question raised in the present case. The matter was addressed by the British Columbia Court of Appeal in Middelkamp v. Fraser Valley Real Estate Board (1992), 96 D.L.R. (4th) 227 (B.C. C.A.). McEachern C.J.B.C. said: “In my judgment, this privilege protects documents and communications created for such purposes both from production to other parties to the negotiation and to strangers, and extends as well to admissibility, and whether or not a settlement is reached. This is because, as I have said, a party communicating a proposal related to settlement, or responding to one, usually has no control over what the other side may do with such documents. Without such protection, the public interest to encourage settlements would not be served.” (Emphasis added) I agree that the said exhibits are not admissible for the purposes of this application. In Hansraj v. Ao, 2002 ABQB 385, 2002 CarswellAlta 627, 314 A.R. 262, 4 Alta. L.R. (4th) 124; additional reasons at 2002 ABQB 772, 2002 CarswellAlta 1064, 314 A.R. 283, 4 Alta. L.R. (4th) 147; additional reasons at 2003 ABQB 299, 2003 CarswellAlta 508, 16 Alta. L.R. (4th) 296, Slatter J. gave a thorough overview of the law relating to correspondence marked “without prejudice”. At pp. 729-735, His Lordship said: It is clear that privileged correspondence may not be used in evidence unless the privilege is waived by the appropriate party. Where an affidavit contains such privileged correspondence, it will be struck from the affidavit. There are generally three types of privilege encountered in everyday litigation. The first privilege is that which attaches to communications relating to legal advice between solicitor and client. This privilege is recognized by the law because of the importance of allowing full and frank correspondence between a solicitor and his or her client. For the privilege to attach, there need only be correspondence between the solicitor and client for the purpose of seeking or giving legal advice: R. v. McClure, [2001] 1 S.C.R. 445, 195 D.L.R. (4th) 513, 151 C.C.C. (3d) 321, ¶ 31-37 (S.C.C.). It is not necessary that any litigation be in existence or contemplated, or that the correspondence be in furtherance of litigation. The privilege in question belongs to the client, and can only be waived by the client. The second and separate common type of privilege is the so-called litigation privilege. It attaches to documents that have been produced for the dominant purpose of furthering litigation: Opron Construction Co. v. Alberta (1989), 71 Alta. L.R. (2d) 28 (Alta. C.A.). In order for this privilege to attach, it is necessary that there be litigation existing or contemplated. It is not a requirement of this type of privilege that solicitor-client communication be involved. The privilege is again the privilege of the client, and must be waived by the client. This type of privilege, like the privilege over solicitor and client communications, can be waived expressly or by knowingly giving a copy of the privileged document to one's opponents, or by attempting to rely on the privileged document to obtain some relief from the Court. This is commonly done, for example, when expert reports are used in Court. The third type of privilege attaches to communications in furtherance of settlement. The law encourages settlement, and accordingly permits the parties to exchange correspondence with a view to resolving their disputes: Costello v. Calgary (City) (1997), 53 Alta. L.R. (3d) 15, 152 D.L.R. (4th) 453, [1998] 1 W.W.R. 222, 209 A.R. 1 (Alta. C.A.). This correspondence may not be used in evidence if the settlement efforts fail. On the other hand, if an agreement of settlement is reached, the correspondence can be used to prove the settlement contract. The privilege that attaches to correspondence in furtherance of settlement belongs to both parties, and it cannot be unilaterally waived by either one of them. This appeal is primarily concerned with the last type of privilege. It follows that the Defendant cannot, simply by attaching the correspondence to an Affidavit and relying on it when seeking relief, waive the privilege. The privilege can only be waived by both parties. However, in order for the privilege to attach in the first place, the correspondence must truly be in furtherance of settlement. Costello quoted with approval the passage in Sopinka and Lederman, The Law of Evidence in Canada, (2d ed., 1992) at para. 14.207 setting out the three conditions for the attachment of this privilege: (a) A litigious dispute must be in existence or within contemplation; (b) The communication must be made with the express or implied intention that it would not be disclosed to the Court in the event negotiations failed; and (c) The purpose of the communication must be to attempt to effect a settlement. Specifically, settlement privilege does not attach to a correspondence simply because it is marked “without prejudice.” On the other hand, if the correspondence is truly in furtherance of settlement and privileged, it makes no difference that the letter is not marked “without prejudice”: Phillips v. Rodgers (1988), 62 Alta. L.R. (2d) 140, 92 A.R. 353, 29 C.P.C. (2d) 193; … Where the parties are engaged in settlement discussions it is undoubtedly a good practice to mark correspondence “without prejudice”, as is the corresponding practice of marking letters “with prejudice” when there is a specific intent to fix legal rights, but the practice is not necessary. Therefore, it is not conclusive that the disputed correspondence on this appeal was in fact marked “without prejudice”. Some of the authorities suggest that marking a letter “without prejudice” is prima facie proof that a letter is privileged, or creates some presumption to that effect. The strength of this presumption, if it ever existed, has unfortunately been considerably weakened by the practice of insurance adjusters and, indeed, many lawyers, of marking every piece of paper that leaves their office “without prejudice.” Where such a practice is evident, there is no basis for applying any presumption of privilege, and the contents of the correspondence must be examined to see if any privilege actually exists. The notation becomes, at best, some evidence of the intentions of the writer on the second part of the test, namely that the document will be kept confidential. … The third branch of the test in Costello is that the communication must be in “an attempt to effect a settlement.” The question is how closely the correspondence has to be to the settlement efforts to attract the privilege. … Correspondence which contains an actual settlement offer is clearly privileged. So, too, would be correspondence that invites compromise, or outlines approaches that might be taken to settlement, or refers in some other indirect way to settlement, even if it did not contain an actual offer of settlement. … The reason for the privilege in the first place is that the law encourages settlement, and effective negotiations require that the parties be able to exchange full and frank views without the fear that their comments would be held against them later. There is no reason for the privilege to attach to merely routine correspondence. The privilege is clearly an important one, and in cases of doubt as to whether the correspondence does relate to the negotiations, the Court should undoubtedly err on the side of protecting the privilege. But it goes too far to say that every piece of correspondence that leaves an adjuster's office is privileged. Sopinka and Lederman (supra, para. 14) state the rule as follows:
paragraphs.heading: Alberta Rules of Court – Rule 5 (Part 2)

sentences.text: (1) The Court may modify or waive any right or power under a rule in this Part or make any order warranted in the circumstances if
(a) a person acts or threatens to act in a manner that is vexatious, evasive, abusive, oppressive, improper or tediously lengthy, or
(b) the expense, delay, danger or difficulty in complying with a rule would be grossly disproportionate to the likely benefit.
[59] Rule 5.3 provides the Court with significant discretion to tailor discovery: Rifco Inc (Re), 2020 ABQB 366 at para 54.

[60] In addition to making a procedural order, the Court may, among other things, make a costs award or require an advance payment against costs payable, or “make any other order respecting the action or an application or proceeding the Court considers necessary in the circumstances”: rule 5.3(2).

For example, while the costs to disclose and produce records is typically borne by the producing party, rule 5.3 permits the Court to consider an interim “cost transfer” or “cost shifting”, whereby the requesting party is required to bear some or all of the costs of providing the requested disclosure: 1218388 Alberta Ltd v Reifel Cooke Group Limited, 2019 ABQB 76 at para 56
Sedona Canada 2022, at 324-327 (Principle 12 and commentary)
Practice Note No.
4, s 6.1.4.2; Innovative at para 27.

[61] The potential for transferring costs to the requesting party was expressly considered by the Alberta Law Reform Institute in its consultation work and recommendations leading up to the 2010 enactment of the Rules: Alberta Law Reform Institute, “Alberta Rules of Court Project, Document Discovery and Examination for Discovery Consultation Memorandum No.

(2002) at para 71 [ALRI Consultation Memorandum 12.2]: “The issue of who bears the responsibility for costs of additional searches is in the court’s discretion and thus may be apportioned based on the particular circumstances of the action.” [62] Borrowing, in part, from the helpful commentary in Sedona Canada 2022 and the ULCC Report (Part 8), the authorities cited therein, other decisions of this Court, and application by analogy of some of the principles set out in rule 10.33(2), non-exhaustive factors to consider in determining whether to require the requesting party to pay all or some of the costs of providing the requested production may include:
(a) whether parties engaged in, or attempted to engage in, joint discovery planning and consultation to find creative or cost-efficient solutions both generally and specific to the request
(b) whether the parties failed to propose or refused to agree to reasonable solutions to the request
(c) whether the parties failed to follow discovery principles in the Rules or common law
(d) whether the parties’ conduct has increased the burden or cost to implement the request
(e) the specificity or scope of the request
(f) the importance and materiality of the requested records
(g) the necessity of the requested records and whether they are available from other sources
(h) the accessibility of the requested records
(i) the availability of technology to reduce costs to one or both of the parties
(j) the burden and costs associated with identifying, collecting, compiling/processing and reviewing the requested records
(k) the producing party’s ability to bear the burden and costs of responding to the request
(l) the relative cost of disclosure and production compared to the amount or importance of the issues in dispute in the litigation
(m) any agreements of the parties respecting records production; and
(n) whether any penalties are imposed against the parties.

Sanctions for Deficient Records Disclosure and Production [63] Another control in the self-discovery system is the potential for “the usual sanctions” for failing to comply with discovery obligations (over and above a costs award): CNOOC v 801 Seventh at para 26.

The Rules provide courts with several tools to sanction non-compliance: rule 5.12 (breach of rules 5.5 or 5.10, or an order under rule 5.11), rule 1.5(6), rule 10.49 (non-compliance with the Rules), and rule 10.52 (contempt of court).
There may also be costs consequences associated with non-compliance: Go Community Centre at paras 193-198.
One Must Produce “Relevant” Records In Tolko Industries Ltd. v.
Railink Ltd., 2003 ABQB 349, 2003 CarswellAlta 559, 333 A.R.
L.R.
(4th) 388, Slatter J. considered the concepts “relevant and material” at pp.
392-393: This relatively new rule has been the subject of some judicial interpretation.
Counsel referred to my recent decision in Weatherill Estate v.
Weatherill, 2003 ABQB 69; [(2003), 11 A.R.
L.R.
(4th) 183 (Q.B.)] where I observed: In determining whether a document is relevant and material, the starting point is the pleadings.
The pleadings define the issues, and relevance must be determined with respect to the issues.
The pleadings are also relevant with respect to the issue of materiality.
However, with respect to materiality one must also have regard to the issue in question.
Where does the burden of proof lie?
Is the issue something that is capable of direct proof, or is it something like a person's state of mind, which can only be proven indirectly?
Does one party essentially have to try and prove a negative?
How are cases of this type usually proven at trial?
The less amenable a fact is to direct proof, the wider will be the circle of materiality.
There are some facts that can only be proven by essentially eliminating all the competing scenarios, thereby leaving the fact in issue as the sole logical inference.
When a state of mind is in issue, it can generally only be proven by demonstrating a pattern of conduct of the person whose state of mind it is.
In deciding whether a particular document is material, one must take a very pragmatic view, viewing the situation from the perspective of the party who must prove the fact in question.

At an interlocutory stage of proceedings, the Court should not measure counsels' proposed line of argument too finely; if counsel can disclose a rational strategy in which the disputed document plays a material part, that should be sufficient.
Again it must be remembered that the purpose of the Rule was to avoid abusive, excessive, and unnecessarily expensive discovery, not to cut off legitimate lines of inquiry.
That relevance is determined by the pleadings, while materiality is more a matter of proof can be seen by the wording of the Rule.
The Rule talks about records that can “help determine” an issue, or that can “ascertain evidence” that will determine an issue.
These are words of proof, and materiality must be determined with that in mind.
The issue is therefore whether the questions that the Tolko officer declined to answer are relevant and material to the contributory negligence defence in the context of the Rules.
Counsel also referred to the decision of Master Funduk in Franco v.
Hackett (2000), 262 A.R.
127 at para.
34: But the test is relevant and material.
That now cuts out the old fishing expeditions.
There is no fishing without first evidence that there are fish in the pond and a reasonable amount of fish.
Defendant has not satisfied me of that.
Conjecture is not sufficient.
This statement has caused counsel in subsequent cases to embark on all sorts of piscatorial analogies.
The metaphor is helpful if one remembers that with respect to the scope of discovery of the parties the question of “whether there are fish” is determined by the pleadings.
If one of the parties pleads that there are or are not fish, then that is determinative of the issue as far as discovery goes.
As to whether there are “a reasonable amount of fish”, that relates to materiality.

Rule 186 says that there are a reasonable amount of fish if there are enough to significantly help determine one or more issues, or to ascertain evidence that can significantly help determine an issue.
Under the new Rule fishing expeditions are still permitted if they fall within that test.
In Mustard v.
Brache, 2006 ABCA 265, 2006 CarswellAlta 1199, 397 A.R.
L.R.
(4th) 203, the Court said, at p.
206: Rule 186.1 was intended to narrow the scope of discovery from what it was previously: Johnston v.
Bryant (2003), 327 A.R.
It was also “designed to limit … tertiary lines of inquiry”: Auer v.
Lionstone Holdings Inc.
The rule makes clear that the parties' pleadings are the basis for determining relevance and materiality.

Discovery of records is now confined to eliciting facts of primary relevance, i.e., facts that are directly in issue, or of secondary relevance, i.e., facts from which the existence of the primary facts may be directly inferred.
Both primary and secondary relevance are determined by reference to the issues raised by the pleadings.
Records seeking information that could reasonably be expected to lead to facts or records of secondary relevance need not be produced.

In addition to being relevant within the meaning of Rule 186.1, records must also be material, that is, they must be reasonably expected to significantly help determine one or more of the issues raised in the pleadings.
The materiality of evidence refers to its pertinency or weight in relation to the issue it is adduced to prove: Black's Law Dictionary, (6th ed.

Records may be relevant within Rule 186.1, but, either alone or in combination with other evidence, be of no significant help to the examining party in proving a fact in issue: NAC Constructors Ltd. v.

(a) whether appropriate inquiries have been made to identify what records are within the possession or power to produce of the litigant, and
(b) whether the appropriate documents have been identified in the affidavit of records.

Where the witness did not participate in the creation of the list of documents and was not involved in the circumstances that gave rise to the claim, and where the answers to questions are frequently, in essence, “I don't know”, the questioning lawyer is, to a great extent, essentially asking questions “in the blind”.

Epp, 2018 ABQB 933, 2018 CarswellAlta 2740, Justice Hughes said: [17]… I note that the Supreme Court of Canada has described solicitor-client privilege as a substantive rule: Alberta (Information and Privacy Commissioner) v University of Calgary, 2016 SCC 53 (CanLII) at para 38.

Our Court of Appeal also has adopted this view, saying this at paras 17-18 of Bre-X Minerals Ltd (Trustee of) v Verchere, 2001 ABCA 255 (CanLII): The Supreme Court has consistently commented that solicitor-client privilege is an important cornerstone to the effective representation of clients by counsel.
That court has gone as far as to characterize solicitor-client privilege as a “fundamental civil and legal right …”: Solosky v.
The Queen, 1979 CanLII 9 (SCC), [1980] 1 S.C.R.

It should be emphasized that solicitor-client privilege is not merely a rule of evidence but a substantive rule, which protects the client's fundamental right to confidentiality. … this privilege casts a wide protective net over communications between solicitors and their clients and is protected zealously by the courts.
(ii) Overview In 0678786 BC Ltd. v.

Bennett Jones LLP, 2021 ABCA 62, 2021 CarswellAlta 339, additional reasons 2021 ABCA 197, leave to appeal refused 2021 CarswellAlta 2491 (S.C.C.), the Court of Appeal gave this overview of the law of privilege: [21] Solicitor and client privilege is a well-established feature of Canadian law.

It is considered to be a substantive principle of fundamental importance to the Canadian legal system, because it allows clients to fully and frankly discuss their legal issues with their counsel, without fear of those discussions and the resulting advice being revealed: Canada (National Revenue) v Thompson, 2016 SCC 21 at para.
17, [2016] 1 SCR 381; Alberta (Information and Privacy Commissioner) v University of Calgary, 2016 SCC 53 at para.
This is essential to the proper functioning of the legal system.
[22] Solicitor and client privilege is recognized as a “class” privilege: Maranda v Richer, 2003 SCC 67 at para.

Solicitor and client privilege does not have to be established factually on a case-by-case basis, because it attaches to the solicitor and client relationship itself: R. v McClure, 2001 SCC 14 at para.
35, [2001] 1 SCR 445; Lizotte v Aviva Insurance Company of Canada, 2016 SCC 52 at paras.
It follows that the client does not have to prove prejudice or provide any objectively reasonable basis for the assertion of the privilege.
Likewise, a person seeking to obtain privileged information cannot argue unfairness, inconvenience, relevance, fiduciary duty, or prejudice as an exception to solicitor and client privilege.
Thus, there is no room here for balancing the relative “fairness” to the two clients (Voorheis and the McCann corporations) of maintaining the privilege over the notes: Lizotte at para.
39, McClure at para.
[23] There are rare recognized exceptions to solicitor and client privilege: a) in the criminal context, “innocence at stake”, as in R. v Brown, 2002 SCC 32 at paras.
3-4, [2002] 2 SCR 185; b) a clear and imminent threat of serious bodily harm or death, as recognized in Smith v Jones, 1999 CanLII 674 (SCC), [1999] 1 SCR 455 at paras.
74–85; and c) communications in furtherance of a criminal purpose, as in Descôteaux v Mierzwinski, 1982 CanLII 22 (SCC), [1982] 1 SCR 860 at p.
893 and R. v Campbell, 1999 CanLII 676 (SCC), [1999] 1 SCR 565 at para.
Lizotte suggested at para.
42 that there might be further exceptions to litigation privilege, which is a distinct form of privilege.
However, a general exception of “urgency or necessity” would not be consistent with the fundamental purposes of solicitor and client privilege.
As noted, relative “fairness” does not provide an exception.
[24] The privilege belongs to the client, not the lawyer.
It follows that the privilege can only be waived by the client: Thompson at para.
The actions of the client may sometimes amount to a waiver, but actions by the lawyer not authorized by the client cannot amount to waiver by the client.
Sometimes privileged documents will come into the hands of third parties.
Whether inadvertent disclosure amounts to waiver depends on the circumstances.
Whether there has been waiver in this case is the central issue of this appeal, discussed infra, paras.
40ff.
[25] Solicitor and client privilege accrues to the benefit of all clients.
The scope of the privilege is not changed because the client in this appeal (Voorheis) is a law firm.
Law firms who retain counsel to provide legal advice enjoy the same rights as other clients: see IOOF Holdings Ltd v Maurice Blackburn Pty Ltd., [2016] VSC 311 at paras.
83, 92, 132-33; Somatra v Sinclair Roche & Temperley, [2000] 1 WLR 2453 at para.
Of course, at a factual level, Voorheis being a law firm generated the circumstances in which privilege came to be an issue, but the basic principles are unchanged.
See also Stuart Olson Construction Inc. v.

254 at 260]… the Supreme Court of Canada approved the following general statement respecting the law of privilege.
The four conditions that must exist before privilege is extended are: (1) The communications must originate in a confidence that they will not be disclosed.
(2) This element of confidentiality must be essential to the full and satisfactory maintenance of the relation between the parties.
(3) The relation must be one which in the opinion of the community ought to be sedulously fostered.
(4) The injury that would inure to the relation by the disclosure of the communications must be greater than the benefit thereby gained for the correct disposal of the litigation.
In Solosky v.
Canada, [[1980] 1 S.C.R.

821 …] the Supreme Court of Canada addressed the issue of the legal professional privilege: The direct communication between a solicitor and client is protected from disclosure by legal professional privilege.
The privilege can only be claimed document by document.
Each document in which legal professional privilege is claimed must:
(i) be communicated between solicitor and client
(ii) entail the seeking or giving of legal advice; and
(iii) be intended to be confidential by the parties. … Solicitor-client privilege protects such communications unless the privilege is waived.
A waiver may occur intentionally by the client expressly waiving it.
Waiver may also occur under some circumstances by implication.

Where there is a waiver, either intentionally or by implication, a disclosure of all or part of what was communicated under the umbrella of privilege may have to be disclosed in order to answer the demands of fairness and consistency.
In general, full disclosure is necessary even when the waiver is only a partial one.
This will be so where only by seeing the whole of the communication between the solicitor and the client can fairness and consistency as between the litigants be assured.

L.R.
(4th) 124, Slatter J., at pp.
130-131, gave the following summary of the three types of privilege: As I noted in Hansraj v.
Ao et al., [2003] A.R.
TBEd.
AP.106, 4 Alta.
L.R.
725 (Q.B.), there are three types of privilege encountered in everyday litigation.
The first privilege is that which attaches to communications relating to legal advice between solicitor and client.
This privilege is recognized by the law because of the importance of allowing full and frank communication between a solicitor and his or her client.
For the privilege to attach, there need only be communication between the solicitor and client for the purpose of seeking or giving legal advice: R. v.
McClure (D.E.), [2001] 1 S.C.R.
It is not necessary that any litigation be in existence or contemplated, or that the correspondence be in furtherance of litigation.
The privilege in question belongs to the client, and can only be waived by the client.
The second and separate common type of privilege is the so-called litigation privilege.
It attaches to documents that have been created for the dominant purpose of furthering litigation: Opron Construction Co. v.
Alberta (1989), 100 A.R.
58, 71 Alta.
L.R.
In order for this privilege to attach, it is necessary that there be litigation existing or contemplated.
It is not a requirement of this type of privilege that solicitor-client communication be involved.
The privilege is again the privilege of the client, and must be waived by the client.

This type of privilege, like the privilege over solicitor and client communications, can be waived expressly or by knowingly giving a copy of the privileged document to one's opponents, or by attempting to rely on the privileged document to obtain some relief from the Court.
This is commonly done, for example, when expert reports are used in Court.
The third type of privilege attaches to communications in furtherance of settlement.
The law encourages settlement, and accordingly permits the parties to exchange correspondence with a view to resolving their disputes: Costello and Dickhoff v.
Calgary (City), [1998] 1 W.W.R.
L.R.
This correspondence may not be used in evidence if the settlement efforts fail.
On the other hand, if an agreement of settlement is reached, the correspondence can be used to prove the settlement contract.
The privilege that attaches to correspondence in furtherance of settlement belongs to both parties, and it cannot be unilaterally waived by either one of them.
In Canadian Natural Resources Ltd. v.
ShawCor Ltd., 2014 ABCA 289, 2014 CarswellAlta 1582, 580 A.R.
265, 2 Alta.
L.R.

(4th) 581, the Court provided this guidance in relation to litigation privilege: [80] The mere fact that a lawyer directs that all records obtained or created after a certain date must first come to him or her is not sufficient to automatically place all such records within the category of solicitor-client privilege.

Not every form of communication with a solicitor by a client is necessarily covered by solicitor-client privilege: Foster Wheeler Power Co v SIGED Inc, 2004 SCC 18 (CanLII) at paras 37–40, [2004] 1 SCR 456.

The privilege attaches to communications between lawyer and client designed to seek out or give legal advice … … [82] The test for litigation privilege in Alberta is that of “dominant purpose” as described by this Court in Nova, An Alberta Corporation v Guelph Engineering Co
(1984), 1984 ABCA 38 (CanLII), 50 AR 199 [Nova].

The dominant purpose test was explained in Moseley, supra at para 24 as follows: The key is, and has been since this Court adopted the dominant purpose test in Nova, that statements and documents will only fall within the protection of the litigation privilege where the dominant purpose for their creation was, at the time they were made, for use in contemplated or pending litigation.

[emphasis in original] [83] Accordingly, a record will not be protected by litigation privilege simply because litigation was one of several purposes for which the record was created: Dow Chemical, supra at para 38.

In Blank, supra at paras 59-60, the Supreme Court of Canada affirmed the dominant purpose test and emphasized its narrow nature at paras 60-61: The dominant purpose test is more compatible with the contemporary trend favouring increased disclosure … While the solicitor-client privilege has been strengthened, reaffirmed and elevated in recent years, the litigation privilege has had, on the contrary, to weather the trend toward mutual and reciprocal disclosure which is the hallmark of the judicial process.

[84] In addition, it must be remembered that under the dominant purpose test, the focus is on the purpose for which the records were prepared or created, not the purpose for which they were obtained: Ventouris v Mountain, [1991] 1 WLR 607 at 620–622 (Eng CA)
General Accident Assurance Company v Chrusz et al

Pre-existing records gathered or copied at the instruction of legal counsel do not automatically fall under litigation privilege: Bennett v State Farm Fire and Casualty Company, 2013 NBCA 4 (CanLII) at paras 47–51, 358 DLR (4th) 229.
Because the question is the purpose for which the record was originally brought into existence, the mere fact that a lawyer became involved is not automatically controlling.

[85] This very point was made thirty years ago by this Court in Nova, supra at para 20: The only case for exclusion which can be made [on the facts before the court] is for documents which were brought into existence by reason of an intention to provide information to solicitors.
That this is an object is insufficient—such a test provides a cloak where other purposes predominate.
Such a test would clothe material that probably would otherwise have been prepared, and otherwise not privileged, with a privilege intended to serve a narrow interest.

Such a test conflicts with the object of discovery today which is to disclose material provided for other purposes. … [87] We accept that when an investigation is ongoing, records may be created for the dominant purpose of litigation at any point after litigation is contemplated.
And we recognize the case management judge effectively found that litigation would be pursued as of February 4, 2009.

But the purpose behind the creation of a record does not change simply because the record is forwarded to, or through, in-house counsel, or because in-house counsel directs that all further investigation records should come to him or her.
Or even because a decision has been made to pursue litigation.
One must always look to the particular record at issue and determine the dominant purpose behind its creation.

After all, litigation privilege “must be established document by document”: Gichuru v British Columbia (Information and Privacy Commissioner), 2014 BCCA 259 (CanLII) at para 32, citing Keefer Laundry Ltd. v Pellerin Milner Corp. et al., 2006 BCSC 1180 (CanLII) at para 96.

An assertion that something was for the dominant purpose of litigation must always be examined in the context of all the facts, the nature of the records in question and all the real reasons that the records were created.

As described by the Court of Appeal, “[l]egal counsel directed the investigation team to segregate the investigation documents and to endorse all material as privileged and confidential.” The Alberta government sought production of that material, but the learned Chambers judge held that “the dominant purpose for Suncor's conduct of the subject investigation into the Accident was in contemplation of litigation.

This finding invariably and logically leads to the collateral finding that, within the context of Suncor's internal investigation that was carried out in anticipation of litigation, the information and documents created and/ or collected during the internal investigation with the dominant purpose that they would assist in the contemplated litigation, are integrally covered by litigation privilege.” The government appealed, and the Alberta Court of Appeal held that the Chambers judge had cast the net of privilege too widely.
The Court of Appeal said: 28 In our view, this formulation of legal privilege by the chambers judge is overbroad and in error.

Even if the dominant purpose of the internal investigation as a whole was in contemplation of litigation, this does not mean that every document “created and/or collected” during the investigation assumes the mantle of that overarching dominant purpose so as to be clothed with legal privilege.

29 This formulation runs afoul of the approach commended by this court in ShawCor, albeit in the context of the Alberta Rules of Court, whereby each document or group of like documents must be examined.

The inquiry requires examination “document by document” or group of like documents to determine the purpose behind its creation: ShawCor at para 87. … 34 Suncor cannot, merely by having legal counsel declare that an investigation has commenced, throw a blanket over all materials “created and/or collected during the internal investigation” or “derived from” the internal investigation, and thereby extend solicitor-client privilege or litigation privilege over them.

This Court stated in ShawCor, at para 84, that “[b]ecause the question is the purpose for which the record was originally brought into existence, the mere fact that a lawyer became involved is not automatically controlling.” And further, at para 87, the Court stated that “the purpose behind the creation of a record does not change simply because the record is forwarded to, or through, in-house counsel, or because in-house counsel directs that all further investigation records should come to him or her.” 35 First, ShawCor requires that, under the dominant purpose test, the inquiry must focus on the purpose for preparing or creating the material, not the purpose for obtaining it.
Second, it is necessary for the referee to examine each of the contested documents or bundle of like documents to determine whether or not they meet the test of legal privilege.
In doing so, it is necessary to apply a legal definition of the claimed solicitor-client privilege or litigation privilege.

36 Solicitor-client privilege attaches to confidential communications between a client and a legal advisor that are connected to seeking or giving legal advice: Blood Tribe Department of Health v Canada (Privacy Commissioner), 2008 SCC 44 at para 10, [2008] 2 SCR 574; see also Blank v Canada (Minister of Justice), 2006 SCC 39 at paras 26–38, [2006] 2 SCR 319 [Blank].

I agree with Conrad, J.A., that there may be circumstances where litigation privilege is found although no solicitor was involved.

The purpose of granting privilege over documents made in anticipation of litigation is to allow a party to freely prepare its case.

If a party is not afforded the protection provided by litigation privilege, it would be required to forward to its opponent unfavourable information which it has developed while preparing its case.

There are generally three types of privilege encountered in everyday litigation.
The first privilege is that which attaches to communications relating to legal advice between solicitor and client.
This privilege is recognized by the law because of the importance of allowing full and frank correspondence between a solicitor and his or her client.
For the privilege to attach, there need only be correspondence between the solicitor and client for the purpose of seeking or giving legal advice: R. v.
McClure, [2001] 1 S.C.R.
It is not necessary that any litigation be in existence or contemplated, or that the correspondence be in furtherance of litigation.
The privilege in question belongs to the client, and can only be waived by the client.
The second and separate common type of privilege is the so-called litigation privilege.
It attaches to documents that have been produced for the dominant purpose of furthering litigation: Opron Construction Co. v.
Alberta (1989), 71 Alta.
L.R.
(2d) 28 (Alta.
In order for this privilege to attach, it is necessary that there be litigation existing or contemplated.
It is not a requirement of this type of privilege that solicitor-client communication be involved.
The privilege is again the privilege of the client, and must be waived by the client.

This type of privilege, like the privilege over solicitor and client communications, can be waived expressly or by knowingly giving a copy of the privileged document to one's opponents, or by attempting to rely on the privileged document to obtain some relief from the Court.
This is commonly done, for example, when expert reports are used in Court.
The third type of privilege attaches to communications in furtherance of settlement.
The law encourages settlement, and accordingly permits the parties to exchange correspondence with a view to resolving their disputes: Costello v.
Calgary (City) (1997), 53 Alta.
L.R.
1 (Alta.
This correspondence may not be used in evidence if the settlement efforts fail.
On the other hand, if an agreement of settlement is reached, the correspondence can be used to prove the settlement contract.
The privilege that attaches to correspondence in furtherance of settlement belongs to both parties, and it cannot be unilaterally waived by either one of them.
This appeal is primarily concerned with the last type of privilege.
It follows that the Defendant cannot, simply by attaching the correspondence to an Affidavit and relying on it when seeking relief, waive the privilege.
The privilege can only be waived by both parties.
However, in order for the privilege to attach in the first place, the correspondence must truly be in furtherance of settlement.
Costello quoted with approval the passage in Sopinka and Lederman, The Law of Evidence in Canada, (2d ed., 1992) at para.
14.207 setting out the three conditions for the attachment of this privilege:
(a) A litigious dispute must be in existence or within contemplation
(b) The communication must be made with the express or implied intention that it would not be disclosed to the Court in the event negotiations failed; and
(c) The purpose of the communication must be to attempt to effect a settlement.

Specifically, settlement privilege does not attach to a correspondence simply because it is marked “without prejudice.” On the other hand, if the correspondence is truly in furtherance of settlement and privileged, it makes no difference that the letter is not marked “without prejudice”: Phillips v.

Therefore, it is not conclusive that the disputed correspondence on this appeal was in fact marked “without prejudice”.
Some of the authorities suggest that marking a letter “without prejudice” is prima facie proof that a letter is privileged, or creates some presumption to that effect.

The strength of this presumption, if it ever existed, has unfortunately been considerably weakened by the practice of insurance adjusters and, indeed, many lawyers, of marking every piece of paper that leaves their office “without prejudice.” Where such a practice is evident, there is no basis for applying any presumption of privilege, and the contents of the correspondence must be examined to see if any privilege actually exists.

The notation becomes, at best, some evidence of the intentions of the writer on the second part of the test, namely that the document will be kept confidential. … The third branch of the test in Costello is that the communication must be in “an attempt to effect a settlement.” The question is how closely the correspondence has to be to the settlement efforts to attract the privilege. … Correspondence which contains an actual settlement offer is clearly privileged.

So, too, would be correspondence that invites compromise, or outlines approaches that might be taken to settlement, or refers in some other indirect way to settlement, even if it did not contain an actual offer of settlement. … The reason for the privilege in the first place is that the law encourages settlement, and effective negotiations require that the parties be able to exchange full and frank views without the fear that their comments would be held against them later.
There is no reason for the privilege to attach to merely routine correspondence.

The privilege is clearly an important one, and in cases of doubt as to whether the correspondence does relate to the negotiations, the Court should undoubtedly err on the side of protecting the privilege.
But it goes too far to say that every piece of correspondence that leaves an adjuster's office is privileged.
